transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~1h02m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Miles (AtlasBridge Head of ML), Rina Kapoor (Platform Eng), Tomás Alvarez (CFO)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): Medium confidence. Main ask: understand unit costs for conversation workloads, options for predictable latency, and security requirements for shipping a pilot inside Q2.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you fitting this in. Quick intros? We'll go five minutes each and then jump into current workload and numbers.
[00:17] Jordan Miles: Sure, Jordan here — Head of ML at AtlasBridge. We're building a conversational assistant for drivers and dispatch, mostly short multi-turn chat, with occasional long instructions.
[00:28] Rina Kapoor: Rina, platform eng. We care about infra, VPC, and making sure logging and observability are there.
[00:36] Tomás Alvarez: Tomás, CFO. I'll mostly be listening for the cost and procurement path.
[00:42] Priya Nair: Priya from Redwood, infrastructure and performance, happy to dig into batching and KV cache later.

[02:05] Alex Chen: Cool. The agenda is per-token pricing, buffering/batching levers, caching, and the tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and private options. Jordan, can you share the prompt mix and expected qps?
[02:23] Jordan Miles: Yeah so on average we're ~15 tokens per request for short chit-chat, some queries hit 80-120 tokens, and about 30% of requests have a longer 300+ token instruction for route recalc. Peak qps is about 45, average sustained 8-12.
[02:45] Tomás (murmur): Okay, so cost math matters.

[03:10] Alex Chen: Great, that mix actually maps to clear levers. Our hosted per-token list price is X but pilots typically get a discount — per-token pricing aside, you get immediate throughput and no infra ops. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower per-token compute due to reserved GPUs. Private/VPC adds more for management license and on-prem ops.
[03:40] Jordan: Can you give us concrete economics on the batching side? If we batch more aggressively, latency suffers; is there a sweet spot?

[04:05] Priya Nair: Yeah so real-world is noisy. For a 15-token median payload you can run continuous batching at 20-50ms queueing and keep tail latency low. For your 300+ token cases the KV cache/prefix caching gives the biggest wins because repeated context and system prompts don't need to be re-computed. We showed a sample before where caching saved ~30-60% of per-request tokens.
[04:32] Rina: When you say KV cache, do you mean something that sits in the runtime or do we need to host an external redis?
[04:45] Priya: Good question — Redwood runtime supports in-memory KV cache on the GPU node for prefix caching and we also support external cache sharding (e.g., redis/rocks) for larger state. For private deployments customers often bring their own cache in VPC and we wire it in.
[05:06] Jordan: And how reliable is the GPU in-memory cache if we have bursty traffic? Do you evict?
[05:14] Priya: We evict LRU style; we also have cache warming and tiered policies. With dedicated pools you have more control over cache residency because the instances are reserved, so cache hit rates are higher.

[06:00] Tomás: Can you break down the up-front and recurring costs for dedicated vs hosted? I want monthly predictable line items for budget planning.
[06:12] Alex: Sure — hosted is purely usage-based: per-token for generation and per-embedding if you use embeddings, plus optional retention/observability add-ons. Dedicated is a monthly commitment — reserved GPU pools — so you get a lower per-token effective cost but you carry a monthly committed spend that looks like infrastructure rent. Private adds a platform fee + support and potential infra if you host on-prem. We'll send a sheet with modeled scenarios.
[06:40] Rina: Also, is quantization supported? Do you recommend q8/q4x to reduce cost?
[06:49] Priya: We support various quantization profiles; recommended depends on your quality targets. For short turn dialogue q4x often hits a decent tradeoff; for high-fidelity route planning where hallucinations are more costly we recommend FP16 or q8 with guardrails. We'll include recommended quant profiles per model in the packet.

[08:02] Jordan: How do fallbacks work if capacity is constrained — like sudden spikes — do you route to a cheaper model? Does that impact SLA?
[08:12] Alex: Yes, we have smart routing. You can define policies that route by latency targets, cost targets, region, or customer tier. Fallbacks can go to a compatible lower-cost model and there's automatic fallback so your app stays online but with different quality. For mission-critical flows we recommend dedicated pools with burst capacity configured.

[09:15] Rina (typing): Any compliance constraints — SSO and KMS — we need SAML and HSM integration.
[09:22] Alex: We support SSO/SAML. For encryption we integrate with customer KMS (cloud HSM) for Private and Dedicated; hosted can use Redwood-managed keys but we also offer BYOK on enterprise plans. We'll attach SOC2 reports and architecture docs.

[10:10] Jordan: Let's talk numbers. If I take your hosted list price, with our mix — roughly 1.2M requests/month — what's a back-of-the-envelope cost?
[10:22] Priya: Quick mental math: assume average tokens per request ~45 (weighted), at hosted rate Y/token that gives ~Z per month. But note caching reduces billable generation tokens; with a ~40% cache hit on prefixes you could see effective tokens drop to ~27/request. Also batching reduces GPU time cost but doesn't change billable tokens for hosted — it reduces latency and throughput cost on Dedicated. We'll run a spreadsheet and give you three scenarios: conservative/no-cache, expected with cache and batching, and aggressive optimization with quantization/dedicated.
[11:05] Tomás: I'd like to see those three scenarios as monthly line items and a projected per-transaction price and a runway analysis for 12 months.
[11:14] Alex: Absolutely. We'll include best/worst/expected.

[12:00] Jordan: Pilot scope — what would a minimal pilot look like to validate latency and cost?
[12:08] Alex: Typical pilot: 2-week spike test on hosted to validate correctness and latencies with your prompt set; then a short dedicated pilot (1-2 months) if you need guaranteed throughput and lower burn. Pilot should include a small dataset, and we instrument evals and SLOs. Tomás, would procurement accept a 2-month dedicated pilot as a line item?
[12:36] Tomás: Possibly, but we'd need a capped cost and a clear success criteria. If we can't get the expected econs we won't convert.
[12:45] Alex: Fair. We'll propose a capped pilot with a not-to-exceed amount and an acceptance checklist.

[14:00] Rina: I want to ask about observability — token-level breakdowns, per-route dashboards, tracing. We need to attribute cost to teams.
[14:10] Priya: Redwood Console supports per-route/model dashboards and token lineage so you can allocate cost back to product teams. There's a small extra for increased metrics retention windows.
[14:28] Jordan: For our multi-tenant drivers product, can we do per-customer routing? Say customers on plan A get lower latency route.
[14:36] Alex: Yes, routing policies can be per-tenant. You can tier models and routes by contract.

[15:40] (Background: brief cross talk; someone on the customer side says "sorry, parking the CFO question until the end")

[18:00] Alex: On batching specifics — Priya, do you have a rule of thumb for queueing latency acceptable for conversation apps?
[18:08] Priya: For real-time voice/driver feedback you want <150ms added queueing ideally. For pure text chat <250ms can be acceptable. Batching windows in practice 10-60ms for low-latency. If you go to large batch intervals like 200ms you get better GPU utilization but conversational UX suffers.
[18:40] Jordan: Makes sense. We probably need a hybrid: short window for driver messages, longer window for background route recalcs.

[20:00] Tomás: If we pick dedicated, what does provisioning timeline look like?
[20:08] Alex: Dedicated pools can be provisioned in ~2-4 weeks depending on region and capacity. Private/VPC or on-prem will add more time — typically 6-10 weeks with networking, KMS integration, and any air-gap requirements.

[21:30] Jordan: Any recommendations on quantization during pilot? Start hosted FP16 and then test q4x quant and dedicated q4x?
[21:40] Priya: That's sensible. Start with hosted FP16 to validate correctness — some providers do q4x in hosted too but for pilot we usually keep quality high. Then for dedicated run A/B with q4x and measure generation delta and perf improvements.

[23:10] Rina: On the private deployment side, how much of the Redwood control plane remains in our VPC vs managed? We need to know what data leaves the VPC.
[23:22] Alex: For Private we offer a customer-managed control plane option where logs and metadata stay in your VPC; for hosted, some operational metrics are in Redwood but payloads can be configured to not be stored. We'll add exact data flow diagrams.

[25:00] Jordan: Do you have any sample runbooks for cost control? Like token caps, rate limiting, and auto-fallbacks that kick in when a budget threshold passes?
[25:10] Alex: Yes — we provide guardrails. Example: rate-limits per-API-key, token quota buckets, automatic model downgrade after a spend threshold, and emailed alerts. We'll share a runbook template.

[27:00] Tomás: On procurement, we need a simple MSA, an SLA stub, and an invoice schedule. Can you point us to a sample?
[27:10] Alex: We'll send the MSA/terms and a sample SLA. Pricing will be in the spreadsheet and the MSA will include standard data protections.

[29:00] Jordan: Any real customer references in logistics/transportation?
[29:08] Alex: We have a couple—can't disclose everything; we'll share redacted case studies and a contact if acceptable.

[30:40] Priya: Quick note on KV cache sizing — for your mix, if 30-40% of requests reuse a 1KB prefix, you might want ~1-2GB cache residency to get a >60% hit rate. For dedicated pools the residency is stable; for hosted it's more ephemeral unless you pin capacity. We'll include a sizing guide.

[33:15] Jordan: What about multi-region routing; we have drivers across NA and EU—data residency matters for some customers.
[33:25] Alex: You can route regionally. For private you can deploy clusters in target regions. Hosted has regional endpoints and we can set residency policies. We'll include supported regions and latency notes.

[36:00] Rina: Is there a cost delta for streaming vs non-streaming responses? Our UI streams partial results for driver feedback.
[36:08] Priya: Streaming doesn't change billable tokens but it can slightly increase overhead due to connection management. For high qps streaming you should size worker threads. We'll note any recommended concurrent connection limits.

[38:00] Tomás: Let's make sure the pilot acceptance criteria are explicit. For me, cost per active session under $X and 95th percentile latency under Y ms."
[38:12] Alex: Agreed — we'll draft a short acceptance checklist: cost control, latency SLOs, cache hit target, and stability under a small spike.

[40:00] Jordan: Any gotchas about cached context and privacy? If we cache prefixes with PII is that an issue?
[40:12] Priya: If prefixes contain PII you should treat them as sensitive; we can avoid persisting PII to disk and honor TTLs. For private deployments you can keep caches in VPC only. We'll add guidance.

[43:00] (Quiet — folks reviewing spreadsheet Alex shared on screen)

[45:00] Alex: Wrapping up, recap of what we promised to send: pricing scenarios (hosted/dedicated/private), pilot proposal with capped spend, SOC2/KMS/VPC docs, runbook template, and KV cache sizing. We'll also set up the KV tech deep-dive next week.
[45:26] Jordan: Sounds good. Can we target April 2 for the pricing packet?
[45:32] Alex: Yes.
[46:00] Tomás: If the packet shows the dedicated model reduces unit cost by 35% within our commit, I'm inclined to sign a pilot. If not, we'll stay hosted and optimize with caching.
[46:12] Priya: Understood. We'll model that in the scenarios.

[50:00] Quick side discussion about logging retention; Rina asks retention windows and cost impact. Alex notes extra observability retention is an add-on.

[55:00] (Clarifying questions from Jordan about the fallback policy syntax)

[60:00] Alex Chen: Ok last Q — any internal blockers on your side?
[60:10] Tomás: Procurement wants a clean PO process and an initial cap; legal will review MSA but I don't expect surprises.
[60:22] Jordan: I'll compile the sample prompts and traffic distribution and shoot them to Priya.
[60:30] Alex: Great — we'll follow up with materials and get the tech deep-dive on the calendar. Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
